newsitem.title: USA: Dollar stretches gains, ends in plus column in US.
newsitem.headline: Dollar stretches gains, ends in plus column in US.

text.p: The dollar closed mostly higher in the U.S. as fresh signs of economic weakness overseas contrasted with surging stocks and bonds and generally upbeat economic news in the United States.

The dollar rose first against the yen in Asian trading after the Nikkei 225 stock index plunged over three percent, bringing total losses for the first four trading days of 1997 to nearly seven percent.
That weakness helped drive investment to the U.S. asset markets, lifting the Dow Jones industrials 76 points higher and boosting the U.S. 30-year Treasury bond more than a point.
Those gains triggered heavy purchases of dollars for yen, currency traders said.

"What's most significant right now is the relative strength of the U.S. stock market compared to Japan. There seems to be some sort of asset shift going on between the two countries," said Thomas Arnold, chief currency dealer at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank in New York.

Later in the session a report showing German unemployment had risen to a record high in December sent the dollar to a fresh two-year high against the German mark and a 30-month high versus the Swiss franc.
By contrast, economists polled by Reuters expect a report on Friday to show healthy U.S. nonfarm payrolls growth of 192,000 in December.
In addition, a report on Thursday showed the U.S. producer price index, excluding food and energy, rose only 0.1 percent in December, bolstering dollar investment.
"People are focusing on many different things, but clearly the dollar overall is moving higher," said Jeffrey Yu, senior currency dealer at Sanwa Bank Ltd New York.
The dollar rose to 116.35/40 yen from 116.17/22 at the open and to 1.5760/70 marks from 1.5748/53.
The U.S. currency rose to 1.3690/00 Swiss francs versus 1.3650/55. The British pound rose to $1.6985/90 from $1.6930/40. The dollar stood little changed at Canadian $1.3521/26 from C$1.3519/24.
Despite its gains, the dollar failed to sustain an early push above 1.58 marks and many traders cited rumors that European central banks had intervened in the market to sell dollars at that level.
As the mark weakens against its European counterparts, exports from other European countries become more expensive, prompting official concern.
"There was decent dollar selling around 1.58 marks and we heard rumors of central bank selling interest up there," said John Beerling, chief currency dealer at Norwest Bank in Minneapolis.
Traders also said an overnight report that U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated his oft-stated desire for a "strong" dollar helped bolster the U.S. currency.
Several Japanese officials earlier in the week publicly warned the dollar was rising too quickly against the yen, fueling sharp dollar losses.
But the losses stopped after two days of silence, with market players no longer worrying about potential open-market dollar sales by Japanese authorities, dealers said.
"Even if Japan were to sell only a modest amount (of dollars), it could send the dollar much lower and I don't think they want that kind of chaos at this point," Yu said.
In other trade, the Australian dollar rose to $0.7810/15 at the close from $0.7789/94 at the open.
((--Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664))
